description:
Found while writing fz-5xp.14's String module.

    fn to_atom(s), do: Atom.from_binary(s)

`Atom.from_binary/1` does not exist. Instead of an unresolved-callee
diagnostic naming it, every program compiled with that module in the runtime
library failed with:

    error[internal/post-resolution-leftover]: quoted function decode failed:
      invalid any value ref: ExpectedTag { expected: ValueKind(15), found: ValueKind(3) }
      --> <generated>

An atom expected, a struct found, at `<generated>` -- no file, no line, no
name. Finding the cause took a bisection of the module.

fz DOES diagnose this properly for ordinary user code:

    error[lower/unbound]: compiler2 lowering found unresolved direct runtime
      callee `Keyword.get/2`   --> /tmp/kw.fz:3:7

so the resolution path knows how to say it. Something on the RUNTIME-LIBRARY
path reaches quoted-function decode with an unresolved callee still in hand,
where user code is refused earlier.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE TYPO: the runtime library is the code most likely to
name a function that does not exist yet, because it is written alongside the
primitives it needs. This is the diagnostic that should catch a half-finished
module, and instead it is the one that hides it.

comments.text:
SECOND INSTANCE, same message, different cause -- which is the point.

    extern "fz" fn fz_binary_to_atom(any) :: atom

`atom` is not one of the extern return types (`ExternTy` has Binary, CString,
I64, F64, Any, Unit). Declaring it produced the SAME error as the unresolved
call, with the same empty location:

    error[internal/post-resolution-leftover]: quoted function decode failed:
      invalid any value ref: ExpectedTag { expected: ValueKind(15), found: ValueKind(3) }
      --> <generated>

Two unrelated mistakes in a runtime-library module -- a call to a function that
does not exist, and an extern return type that is not supported -- are
indistinguishable at the surface, and neither names the module, the function or
the line. Both cost a bisection to find.

So this is not one missing diagnostic; it is a path with NO diagnostic, where
every way of being wrong arrives as the same internal decode failure. Whatever
fix lands should make the two say different things, and both should name where
they are.

title: A call to a non-existent function in a runtime-library module is an internal decode error, not a diagnostic
